newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Duma urges economic sanctions on Latvia.
newsitem.headline: Russian Duma urges economic sanctions on Latvia.

text.p: Russia's State Duma lower chamber of parliament called on Friday for economic sanctions to be imposed against Latvia and accused the Baltic state of violating the rights of Russians living there.

A statement adopted by the opposition-dominated legislature appealed to the Russian government and President Boris Yeltsin to introduce the sanctions and keep them in place until Latvia improves its treatment of the Russian speakers.
The non-binding appeal, adopted by 230 votes to 11, was in protest against a declaration on August 22 by the Latvian parliament "on the occupation of Latvia".
The declaration called on the international community to recognise the fact of Latvia's occupation by the Soviet Union in 1940.

The Russian Duma, dominated by communists and nationalists, said in its statement that this document, described as "anti-Russian" and "provocative", distorted the truth about the incorporation of Latvia into the Soviet Union.
It said the Soviet parliament had agreed on August 5, 1940, to a request by the "Latvian Soviet Socialist Republic" to become part of the Soviet Union.
The Russian statement said the Latvian parliament's move stirred ethnic tension and showed that the Baltic state intended to give its Russian-speaking population the status of "occupation citizens".
Hundreds of thousands of Russian speakers were stranded in the three Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia after they regained independence from the former Soviet Union in 1991.
Many of them are deeply nostalgic for the past, when they felt secure in the Soviet empire.

Most Russians in Latvia and Estonia do not have citizenship and say they have been deliberately shut out of political life. Balts say the masses of Russians who came to their countries during the 50 years of Soviet rule were illegal immigrants.
They say they should go through a formal naturalisation procedure and prove their commitment to the new republics.
In Lithuania, where the Russian minority is much smaller, everyone was given citizenship.
